A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSkips research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary sections are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original optical-flow and classification experiments on DSEC-flow, DVS128 Gesture, SHD, and SSC, alongside ablations, convergence analyses, and energy estimates.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds CIFAR10-DVS experiments, inference-time skip-removal analyses, spike-activity observations, and experiments across random seeds.

M1.justification: The core delayed connections, adaptive LIF neurons, alpha mixing, NAS procedure, and training algorithm are retained. Sections 4.5 and 5 introduce an optional deployment procedure that disables delayed-state propagation at inference. For DSEC-flow, Appendix B.2 explains retaining the alpha-weighted current-state contribution while zeroing the delayed contribution.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original datasets and adds CIFAR10-DVS object classification in Section 4.6. This extends coverage to a distinct recognition task and event streams with artificially generated temporal information from repeated camera movements.

E2.justification: DVS-Gesture Table 2 adds Streaming rollout SNN, cited as Kugele et al. (2021), with 0.8M parameters and 95.56% accuracy. The new CIFAR10-DVS comparison adds NDA ResNet18/VGG11 baselines, alpha-SSA, and SpikingResformer, alongside Spikingformer. The original optical-flow and speech comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation using large spiking ResNet18/VGG11 models with NDA augmentation, and controlled inference tests that replace delayed-state inputs with zeros. Table 12 additionally evaluates NAS searches producing seed-dependent delay and connection choices. The original datasets' stated splits, metrics, sequence lengths, and training schedules are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Figure 8 add spike-activity analyses for two SHD examples. Appendices B.2 and C.2 test whether gains survive disabling temporal skips at inference, while Appendix D.2 examines robustness across NAS seeds. The earlier delay, placement, depth, energy, convergence, and operator analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides benchmark point estimates without reported seed counts or dispersion. v2 explicitly reports additional DSEC-flow NAS experiments across three random seeds, with mean AEE and standard deviation in Table 12. This introduces uncertainty reporting for that evaluation, without establishing repeated-run reporting for all benchmarks.

E6.justification: The original headline scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results: CIFAR10-DVS backward-TSkips ResNet18 reaches 82.93% versus its 78.00% baseline; SHD backward-TSkips-1 scores 92.78% with skips disabled versus 93.64% enabled; and Table 12 reports seed-aggregated AEE. These are new evaluations, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions. New Table 6 reverses Mini/Micro labels relative to Table 1.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the formal temporal constraint from t < Delta t < T to 0 < t - Delta t < T and explicitly specifies discrete time indices. This revises the admissible delayed-time condition. The principal equations and search-space calculation remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, enumerated contributions, headline performance claims, and conclusion retain their substantive message. However, v2 removes the introduction's assertion that learnable synaptic delays capture only short-window patterns, narrowing the comparative claim motivating TSkips.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the skip-removal results as evidence that TSkips improve learned representations during training, and discusses differences between forward and backward spike activity. New discussion addresses historical-state storage, memory and energy costs, neuromorphic routing constraints, and deployment without delayed states. Section 4.6 also acknowledges the parameter-efficiency advantage of competing transformers.

D1.justification: v2 documents the zero-tensor inference control, its treatment of alpha on DSEC-flow, and per-run NAS-selected delays and positions. Existing hardware, optimizer schedules, neuron initialization, dropout, and detailed architecture tables are retained. Corresponding CIFAR10-DVS-specific skip placements and delays are not supplied.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive discussion of streaming rollouts, SCTT temporal skips, and TTFS delayed connections. It replaces the blanket short-window characterization with distinctions involving configuration-search expense, synchronization, and evaluation scope. Section 4.4 also positions TSkips as complementary to DCLS-Delays. These changes materially refine the relationship to closely related research.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the order of the original methodological and experimental material are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory rewrites, introduces Observations, Scalability, and Discussion sections, and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A-D. Author information, citation style, terminology, and cross-references are also updated.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a predominantly single-column journal layout, extensively resizing and relocating figures and tables. v2 adds the spike-activity Figure 8 and Tables 4, 6, 9, and 12. Existing plots and supplementary tables remain identifiable despite renumbering and reformatting.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through inference-removal controls, three-seed NAS results, and evaluation on standard architectures for CIFAR10-DVS. Closer engagement with prior temporal-skip methods and explicit hardware limitations also improve scientific positioning and qualification of the claims. These are substantial gains beyond the retained headline scores. The inconsistent Mini/Micro labels in Table 6 and missing CIFAR10-DVS skip configurations limit precision and reproducibility, but do not outweigh the overall improvement.
